extracted.intended_audience: naturalists, evolutionary biologists, and educated readers of natural history interested in sexual selection and comparative anatomy
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and lines of evidence for inferring the origin, function, and evolution of sexually dimorphic weapons (horns, tusks, canines, size differences) in mammals and other animals. Focuses on comparative, developmental, behavioral, and experimental indicators used to judge whether a character is sexually selected and how it has changed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sex-limited transmission / inheritance patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: The way a character is transmitted between the sexes (e.g., always through the female) indicates latent capacity and inheritance; this affects whether a weapon appears in one or both sexes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If horns or other weapons are 'always transmitted through the female' and females retain a latent capacity (seen in old or diseased females), this suggests inheritance patterns that explain presence/absence in sexes (examples: reindeer females, rudiments in Cervulus moschatus and wapiti). Castration and cross-breeding experiments (Peel’s Lonk × hornless breeds) provide further evidence on sex-linked inheritance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing of development (ontogeny) correlated with sex-expression
rubrics_metrics.description: When a character is developed at an unusually early age (before sexual differences appear) it tends to be expressed in both sexes; when it arises late in life it tends to be limited to the sex in which it first appears.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reindeer horns develop very early, which is linked to their occurrence in both sexes; traits that appear late (size, strength) are often transmitted primarily to males. Use age-of-appearance data (puppy growth rates, deer horn timing) to infer likely sex-limited transmission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative distribution across related species and genera
rubrics_metrics.description: Presence or absence of a character among closely related species or within genera helps determine whether it is primordial or secondarily acquired by one sex.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare many species in the family: if females of most species lack horns, then presence in one species’ females is likely secondary (examples: reindeer among Deer family; antelopes with graduated series from hornless females to equally-horned sexes). Look for mixed conditions within genera as evidence for inheritance rather than adaptive female use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct observation of functional use in combat
rubrics_metrics.description: Observed use of horns, tusks, or canines in fights between males supports their role as sexual weapons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect behavioral accounts of fighting style and weapon use (e.g., rams butting, goats jerking with scimitar-shaped horns, bulls goring and tossing, elk rolling head to plunge antlers). First-hand naturalist reports and hunting/ethological anecdotes are used as supporting evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Behavioral specialization matching morphology
rubrics_metrics.description: The manner in which an animal fights should correspond to the shape and placement of its weapon (species-specific modes of use).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match horn/tusk morphology to described fighting maneuvers (Oryx kneeling to make points forward; Ovis cycloceros uses a cutting jerk; Italian buffalo uses forehead blow). Discrepancies or specializations can indicate historical modifications of fighting style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Castration experiments as tests for sexual character
rubrics_metrics.description: Effects of castration on the development or maintenance of a trait indicate whether it is a sexual character dependent on sex-hormonal constitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If castration reduces or prevents renewal/development of a trait (stags stop renewing horns), it points to sexual dependence; exceptions (male reindeer still renew after castration) may be explained by early developmental timing. Use castration records across species and breeds as diagnostic evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inverse relation between types of weapons (horns vs canines)
rubrics_metrics.description: Presence or elaboration of one kind of weapon (horns) is often inversely related to development of another (canine teeth), suggesting functional replacement during evolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe clades: hornless taxa (camels, musk-deer, chevrotains) often retain large canines; ruminants with horns rarely have functional canines. Infer historical replacement of weapon systems from comparative anatomy.

rubrics_metrics.name: High variability and occasional female expression indicate lability
rubrics_metrics.description: Extreme variability of secondary sexual characters and occasional presence in the opposite sex show these traits are evolutionarily labile and can differ even among close forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use observed variability (female tusks/horns present in some populations; two tusks in some male narwhals; absence in some female walruses) to argue trait lability. Frequent exceptions and regional differences strengthen inference of recent or ongoing change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secondary functions and multifunctionality
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if a trait originated via sexual selection, it may acquire additional uses (feeding, defense, probing), so functional inference must account for multiple roles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document non-sexual uses (elephant probing/stripping trees, bull defending herd, horns breaking fall for ibex/goat). Secondary uses do not preclude sexual origin but must be considered in adaptive explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Morphology not perfectly optimal for defense implies ornamentation
rubrics_metrics.description: When a weapon’s form seems maladapted for ordinary defense or fighting (e.g., highly branched antlers), ornamentation or display may have played a role in its evolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note cases where branched antlers can interlock or be disadvantageous; consider whether upper branches act as protection or ornament. Use human aesthetic analogies cautiously; seek behavioral corroboration of display function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Costly traits (energetic and functional costs) weighed against benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: Large horns/tusks incur energetic costs and handicap in locomotion; persistence implies compensating sexual advantages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantify costs where possible (e.g., tusk weights, moose antler expanse, Irish elk horns vs skull weight) and consider impediments (retarded flight, encumbrance in dense vegetation). Evaluate whether reproductive advantage offsets costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correlation of dimorphism with mating system and male pugnacity
rubrics_metrics.description: Degree of sexual dimorphism in size and weaponry correlates with mating system (polygamous species with male-male combat show greater dimorphism).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare species with polygamous vs monogamous systems (polygamous seals and sperm-whales show large male size and scarring from fights; right-whales less dimorphic). Use ethnological/behavioral accounts to link pugnacity to dimorphism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ontogenetic timing indicates sex-specific inheritance potential
rubrics_metrics.description: Traits acquired late in life are more likely to be transmitted to the same sex; traits arising early may be passed to both sexes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use growth curves and age-of-attainment (Scotch deer-hound males grow later than females; dog puppy weights through weeks) to infer sex-limited inheritance. Late-acquired advantages tested in selection regimes affect male progeny more.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental and breeding evidence (domestication and crosses)
rubrics_metrics.description: Results from breeding, domestication, and crosses illuminate inheritance and sex-expression of traits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: J. Peel’s cross (Lonk × hornless breeds) produced males with reduced horns and hornless females; domesticated breeds showing sex-differential horn presence. Use controlled breeding histories to evaluate heritability and sex-linkage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Directional change and spread of advantageous variants
rubrics_metrics.description: Observation that a novel advantageous form increases in frequency over generations indicates selection favoring that form (sexual or natural).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case of spike-horn bucks in Adirondacks: a novel single-spike morphology provided advantages (speed, effectiveness) and increased in frequency over ~20 years. Track frequency changes in populations to infer selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional mismatch with predation defense argues sexual function
rubrics_metrics.description: When morphology seems ill-suited to defense against predators but suited to male-male combat (or display), sexual selection is the likely primary cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Oryx long backward-pointing horns seem poorly placed for predator defense, but when combined with knee posture they function in male fights; thus infer development via sexual selection rather than predation pressure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fossil and historical measures inform magnitude and cost
rubrics_metrics.description: Fossil measurements and historical records (skull and horn weights, antler span) help assess past extremes and costs of traits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use fossil evidence (Irish elk antlers eight-foot tips, skull weight) and museum specimens to quantify historical trait magnitudes and infer selection pressures and possible constraints.
